text: Go No Go answers one question for NASA technology transfer. Can this patent be licensed, to this company, for this use? A knowledge graph and seven fixed rules decide. The model never does.
This is the ontology, forty-eight classes. Each dot is a kind of thing. Watch the arrows.
A patent is what every license is about.
A grant points at a patent. It comes in two kinds: proposed, and executed.
A signed license adds a licensee, a term, and an exclusivity type.
Fields of use sit in a vocabulary hierarchy. A grant for a broad field covers the narrower ones.
Territories nest the same way. North America covers the United States.
Every fact records when it holds, and when the system learned it, so any past decision can be rerun.
A model can propose a field of use, but it stays a candidate until a person approves it.
A risky or conflicting approval waits for a second person, counsel.
A decision records the facts the rules read, the release, and a signature.
Now provenance. This is the trail behind one approved fact.
Here is the approved fact. Every fact carries its own provenance.
A named person approved it, not a standing policy.
The approval event records the time and the steward's reason.
The fact was derived from a proposal. The proposal stays, unchanged.
Someone proposed it. A proposer can never be the approver.
The proposal itself came from a generator run, labeled synthetic.
And the fact is about one patent. Nothing here was edited or deleted.
Here is how a question becomes a verdict. Fixed steps, and no model deciding.
The parser reads concepts out of the question with fixed patterns, and keeps the span each one came from.
Seven rules run on every request. Each fills a fixed query template and reads the graph.
Proposed facts wait in a candidate graph. No rule reads it, so a proposal cannot change a verdict.
A versioned combiner turns the rule results into one verdict: go, no go, hold, counsel, or no data.
Every decision is stored with its inputs and a signature, so it can be replayed.
A risky approval waits for a second person. A steward cannot approve their own proposal, and counsel must approve any change that would turn a verdict to go.
Each role may read only some graphs. Royalty terms never leave their own graph.
Now the same system on AWS, drawn from the stacks we deployed in Ohio.
A person reaches CloudFront over HTTPS. CloudFront serves the app from a private S3 bucket, and forwards API calls.
API Gateway checks the Cognito token on every call. Cognito holds six role groups, and a user can belong to only one.
The engine Lambda runs the rules and the approval loop. It asks Cedar who may do what, using the same policies that Verified Permissions holds.
Each decision goes to DynamoDB, and a tamper-evident copy goes to S3 under Object Lock. EventBridge carries action events, and one KMS key encrypts the data.

Inside a network with no internet route, a read-only query Lambda is the only path for reads. Only the loader and the step that applies an approved grant may write, and no outside caller can reach either.
New agreements arrive as PDFs. Step Functions has Textract read each one, fixed patterns extract the grant, SHACL checks it, and the workflow waits for a steward before anything reaches the graph.
A budget alarm watches the spend. When the review is done, one script tears everything down, and the public demo keeps running without AWS.
Does the ontology earn its place? Two hundred questions went to four answerers, scored against verdicts fixed by hand.
Go No Go was right ninety-seven and a half percent of the time. A graph agent with the same facts reached seventy-two, and vector search alone, twenty.
The error that matters is a false go: clearing a license that should be blocked. The graph agent made thirty-two. Go No Go made none.
The agent usually found the right agreement, and still misread the rule. That is the case for an ontology. The model reads, and the rules decide.
That is Go No Go. Every verdict has a source. The code, the diagrams, and the guide are on GitHub.
